transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 72 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Quantura ML Infra), Tom Reynolds (Quantura SRE), Elena Park (Quantura CTO)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to reproduce an instability Quantura saw when enabling 4-bit quantization + CUDA Graph capture. Focus: kernel selection differences between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM paths, KV-cache prefetch interactions, and fallback behavior when a quantized kernel can't run under CUDA Graph lockstep. Goal is to align on repro steps and pilot scope.

Topics Covered:
- Repro steps and hardware: nvlink multi-GPU A100x2 config, OS/driver, CUDA 12.x
- TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM kernel choices and what triggers the fallback into slower fp16 or int8 paths
- CUDA Graph capture & replays: when replay becomes non-deterministic with dynamic kv-cache lengths
- KV cache eviction/prefetch and how batching interacts with quantized kernels
- On-prem / VPC considerations: KMS keys for model artifacts and audit logging during pilot

High-level action recap at end.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: All right everyone thanks for carving time, we wanted to follow up on the crash you saw during quantized runs, and walk through a repro.
[00:12] Priya: Yeah thanks, morning. We saw a big latency spike and then a CUDA graph error, it kind of, uh, says "invalid kernel launch" then the process restarts.
[00:22] Luis: ok, can you describe the capture? Was it during warmup or when you hit a long prefix?
[00:27] Tom: It was during steady state, around token 512 range, we have prefix caching enabled. We did persistent kv cache, and then we tried turning on CUDA graph capture in our runner.
[00:36] Luis: persistence + cuda graph + quantization is like the three musketeers of edge cases, yeah. Can you share which quantization config you used? 4-bit groupwise, per-channel?
[00:44] Priya: We used a 4-bit asymmetric per-tensor, group size 64, using the open-quant toolchain that we normally run. Model is an Llama-derived 13B.
[00:52] Luis: cool. And are you forcing the TensorRT-LLM path or running with our auto-kernel selector?
[00:58] Priya: Auto selector, but we pinned a profile that prefers lower latency, so I think it chose the TRT kernels when available.
[01:05] Luis: got it. One thing we've seen is that TRT kernel variants sometimes assume contiguous KV layouts for replayed cuda graphs; when quantization inserts a packing step, the memory layout changes and the cuda-graph replay will try to rebind pointers that... don't match, leading to invalid launches.
[01:20] Elena: so is that a cookie-cutter bug in TRT or is it our setup?
[01:24] Luis: it's a combination. TRT kernels are fast, but the TRT-LLM plugin expects a stable tensor shape and pointer set between capture and replay. If quantized packing runs only at runtime (i.e., not prepacked during compile), the graph capture records a different op sequence. vLLM path tends to be more tolerant because it has a more interpreter-like kernel chain, but it's slower.
[01:42] Tom: We compared runs with vLLM and saw less crashes but 30% slower token throughput.
[01:48] Maya: That's a common tradeoff. Our default heuristic is: prefer TRT when latency budgets are tight, fallback to vLLM when we detect capture instability or memory layout churn. The big question — can we reproduce reliably?
[01:58] Priya: Yes, we have a minimal harness. We capture cuda graphs after warmup, then run a batch of inferences with prefix lengths jittered. It fails more when prefix length varies across the batch.
[02:10] Luis: that aligns with pointer rebinding issues. When prefix length changes you change the KV cache offset; if TRT kernel captured absolute pointers, replay breaks.
[02:19] Elena: Any mitigation short-term? We need a pilot next week.
[02:22] Luis: A few options: 1) force prepack during compile so memory layout is stable; 2) disable cuda-graph for quantized paths; 3) add a compatibility shim that normalizes KV pointers before replay. Each has cost.
[02:34] Maya: For the pilot we usually propose 1) try prepack + TRT, 2) if still flaky, run TRT in a non-captured mode or fallback to vLLM for those sequences, 3) collect traces. We'll share the perf spreadsheet.
[02:46] Tom: Can you explain prepack cost? Is it extra memory or precomputation time?
[02:50] Luis: Prepack moves the quant packing into model load/compile time — it increases startup time and may bump memory slightly but makes runtime stable. The alternative is runtime packing which is cheaper to compile but changes pointer patterns.
[03:03] Priya: Hmm, our service prefers fast cold starts, so more startup penalty is awkward.
[03:08] Maya: That's typical — tradeoffs. For an enterprise pilot we can accept a longer startup for stability.
[03:12] Luis: Also, batching interacts here — if you have dynamic batch sizes, cuda-graph capture usually expects a fixed batch shape. The runtime has a continuous batching layer but capture isn't friendly to variable shapes unless you do multiple captures per shape.
[03:25] Tom: We do variable batching, yes. We thought CUDA graph would buy us 2x throughput but it's brittle.
[03:31] Luis: Right. Another point: KV cache eviction and prefetch. If the runtime evicts older segments and then prefetches into different buffer slots, the underlying pointer arithmetic changes. During capture, that will mismatch.
[03:44] Priya: We saw eviction spikes when load went up. It seemed like a memory threshold.
[03:49] Luis: If you can keep working set under threshold, the persistent cache is fine. Otherwise you want a stable allocation map — that's where pinned allocation and a deterministic allocator help.
[03:59] Elena: Does Redwood's private on-prem image include the deterministic allocator?
[04:03] Maya: We have a toggle in the runtime policy to enable a deterministic allocator for private deployments. We'll include the terraform and runtime flag.
[04:12] Tom: Good. About kernel selection: what exactly differs between TRT-LLM and vLLM here?
[04:17] Luis: TRT-LLM compiles fused attention + ffn kernels optimized for GPU memory locality, it often uses workspace pointers and in-place updates. vLLM's approach is more stage-based: attention, then reorder, then ffn. That staging is slower but pointer-stable.
[04:33] Priya: Is quantization compatibility better with vLLM then?
[04:36] Luis: Empirically yes, vLLM's slower path doesn't assume the same pointer invariants, so graph replay is less likely to break. But as Tom observed, throughput drops.
[04:45] Maya: We also saw that TRT with certain int8 kernels requires per-channel calibration data stored adjacent to tensor buffers; when open-quant produces per-tensor scales these get reorganized and the compiled engine layout differs between runs. That's another source of mismatch.
[04:58] Tom: So calibration artifacts can change engine layout, causing replay to mismatch?
[05:02] Luis: Exactly. The compiled TRT engine embeds kernel choices and also assumes certain scratch buffers sizes. If the quant pipeline changes, the engine might not be compatible across captures.
[05:12] Priya: Ok, for our pilot we could try a controlled run: 1) compile+prepack once, 2) pin batch size, 3) disable eviction by bumping memory, and 4) run with/without cuda graph and compare.
[05:25] Luis: That's the exact repro we want. Also capture nvprof / nsight logs and the cuda graph replay error dump.
[05:31] Maya: Luis, can you outline the exact command flags we'll need?
[05:34] Luis: Sure. I'll send a gist but quick list: --prepack-quant=true --force-trt-engine=on --cuda-graph-capture=on|off for comparisons, --kv-persistence=on, --deterministic-allocator=true, and a runtime env var TRW_RUNTIME_CAPTURE_SHAPE="fixed".
[05:53] Priya: Will you also add a flag for nvlink peer-to-peer check? We saw some cross-GPU memory issues when NVLink was not properly enabled.
[06:01] Luis: Good call. Add --nvlink-peer-check=fast. If nvlink misconfigs, pointer offsets may be different across GPUs.
[06:08] Tom: For the multi-GPU case does CUDA graph capture across devices work?
[06:12] Luis: Cross-device graph capture is supported but trickier — you need unified capture setup and consistent memory addresses. We recommend starting single-GPU repro then scale to NVLink.
[06:22] Elena: The pilot likely needs NVLink though our infra standard is A100-80GB with NVLink.
[06:28] Luis: Then we'll need to ensure peer mappings are stable. We can also run a distributed capture-less mode for the multi-GPU case if graph capture proves too brittle.
[06:36] Priya: Can you elaborate on fallback heuristics? When runtime decides to drop to vLLM or to disable cuda graph?
[06:41] Maya: The runtime tracks capture success rate and kernel failures. If we hit a repeated invalid launch we flip a policy per model-version: disable graph capture and bias away from fused TRT kernels for that traffic slice. We can do canary rollouts per route too.
[06:54] Luis: There's an automatic monitoring check — if token error rate for capture-based mode > 0.1% in 5 minutes we automatically route 20% of traffic to a safer path.
[07:03] Tom: That sounds useful; is it configurable?
[07:05] Maya: Yes, policy is configurable via the console or API. We'll give you defaults for the pilot.
[07:11] Priya: One more question: KMS and audit logs for on-prem pilot — we need to ensure keys don't leave our VPC.
[07:17] Maya: Our private deployment supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; keys stay in your KMS, Redwood just calls via secure peered control plane. We'll share the architecture diagram.
[07:26] Elena: Good. Also, can Redwood capture traces and store them off-box for Redwood to help debug? We prefer logs to stay in our network.
[07:34] Luis: For private deployments you can configure log forwarding to your SIEM; we can also ship sanitized traces, but by default debug traces can stay on your S3 or an internal endpoint.
[07:44] Priya: Ok thank you.
[07:46] Maya: Let's summarize next steps.
[07:48] Luis: I'll prepare the detailed repro flags and a script to run single-GPU then NVLink multi-GPU tests. I'll also include nsight and nvprof capture commands.
[07:58] Priya: We'll run the harness and push results and logs to the shared S3 bucket, link to the spreadsheet.
[08:04] Maya: I will send the pilot contract and indicative pricing, plus a checklist for on-prem network/KMS.
[08:10] Elena: We'll aim to have the infra ready by end of week.
[08:13] Maya: Great. Anything else?
[08:15] Tom: Can you also include a short doc describing safe quant profiles (group sizes and calibration tips)?
[08:20] Luis: Yep, I'll add a short runbook with recommended group sizes and prepack settings.
[08:24] Maya: Cool. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
